shortDescription: Reforms to electricity dispatch rules in Guangdong, China's largest gas power market, are likely to reduce operating hours at gas-fired power plants and slow growth in gas consumption, consultancy Wood Mackenzie said.

children: Reforms to electricity dispatch rules in Guangdong, China's largest gas power market, are likely to reduce operating hours at gas-fired power plants and slow growth in gas consumption, consultancy Wood Mackenzie said.

Before the policy reforms in July 2025, natural gas plants had guaranteed dispatch hours and an approved on-grid tariff. They also received additional subsidies when gas costs rose beyond a certain level. The reforms replaced that system with economic dispatch, requiring gas generators to bid to recover fuel costs.
The change is expected to result in reduced running hours for natural gas power plants.
The changes come amid a ramp-up in renewable power generation. Guangdong's solar and wind capacity rose from 14 gigawatts (GW) to 105 GW between 2020 and 2026.
The "Guangdong model" is a "guide for how China's largest gas power market is adapting to a high-renewable grid," said Kai Dong, Wood Mackenzie's principal analyst for Asia Pacific gas and LNG.
Gas demand could rise if prices fall sharply, but Wood Mackenzie estimates gas would need to drop to about $6/MMBtu to compete with coal, versus recent Asian spot prices near $30/MMBtu.
